conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for coming in today. I’m Dr. Patel, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My whole job is to support new mothers as they adjust to life after baby, and I’m really glad you’re here.

We’re about to use a short questionnaire called the EPDS—short for the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s simply ten questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting or a judgment about you; it’s just a quick snapshot so we can figure out the best ways to support you.

Everything you share is confidential, and we’ll take it at your pace. If any question feels hard, we can pause or talk it through. When we’re done, we’ll go over what the score means and discuss any next steps together.

Ready to begin?  
First, I’d love to know: over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[offers a small, tired smile]  
I can still laugh—just… not as easily as before she was born. It feels like I have to dig a little deeper to find it, and a lot of the time I’m too worn out to even try.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly yes, but sometimes it takes more effort than it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to little things—like when my mom brings over dinner or when I get twenty quiet minutes to shower—but the bigger stuff, like outings or even coffee with friends, feels more like a chore than something I’d enjoy.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times this week. Yesterday she wouldn’t settle for her nap and I kept thinking maybe I’m missing some cue, like if I were more “in tune” she’d sleep and I could get the laundry done. Deep down I know babies just cry, but the thought still pops up that I should be handling it better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart races because I’m sure she’s not breathing—even though she’s right there, perfectly fine. It’s not constant, maybe a few times this week, but it feels silly afterward because nothing’s actually wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had that out-of-nowhere panic, but one night when she wouldn’t stop crying I felt my chest tighten and I had to hand her to my partner for a minute. It passed quickly, but it scared me how fast the stress shot up.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I’m keeping up, but by late afternoon I feel like I’m running on fumes. The other day she had three outfit changes from spit-ups and I almost cried over the extra laundry—just felt like one more thing I couldn’t get to.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really “unhappy,” just… wired. I lie there hearing every little squeak from the bassinet, wondering if she’s about to wake up, running through tomorrow’s to-do list. Most nights I eventually drift off, but it takes a while.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah, I’ve had a couple of evenings where I just felt… flat. Not sobbing or anything, more like a heaviness sits on me and the day feels colorless. It’s not every day, but it’s definitely there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

No, I haven’t actually cried. I’ve felt teary a couple of times, like when I couldn’t get her to latch in the middle of the night, but the tears never quite came. I just felt exhausted and swallowed hard until it passed.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I’m tired, but I want to be here for her. I just need some rest and maybe a clearer head.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wk postpartum, partner present, no self-harm ideation endorsed.

Areas of Significance  
- Anhedonia (loss of anticipatory pleasure)  
- Mild-moderate low mood (“flat,” “colorless” days)  
- Excessive guilt/blame re infant care  
- Episodic anxiety/panic (heart racing, chest tightness)  
- Sleep-onset difficulty linked to rumination, hypervigilance to infant  
- Subthreshold tearfulness, no actual crying spells  
- Feels “running on fumes” afternoons, overwhelmed by routine tasks

Risk Factors  
- Partial anhedonia & low mood → possible depressive spectrum  
- Anxiety symptoms (no avoidance, no compulsions) → possible postpartum anxiety  
- No suicidal/homicidal ideation; no history given → acute safety risk currently low

Screening Impression  
Responses indicate subsyndromal mood and anxiety symptoms impacting coping. Score suggests monitoring warranted; formal assessment (EPDS/PHQ-9/GAD-7) and follow-up in 1–2 weeks recommended to track trajectory and rule out progression to major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder.
